title: What a share really is
desc: Shares, market value, and why the price isn’t what the business is worth

cards.added: Feedback for options the board doesn’t show written for the Academy
cards.title: What do you own?
cards.situation: Northwind Bakery is split into 100 equal shares. You buy 5 of them. What do you own?

options.text: A loan Northwind must pay back
options.feedback: A loan is a bond, and a bond gets paid back. A share is ownership: you own part of the bakery.

options.text: A slice of Northwind: 5% of the company
options.feedback: A share is a slice of the company. Five slices out of 100 is 5%.

options.text: A promise the price will rise
options.feedback: Nobody promises that. A share is ownership: the price can rise or fall, and you share in how the business does.

cards.title: A slice of a real business
cards.text: A company splits its ownership into **[[share|shares]]**. Buy one and you own a small slice of the business, its profits and its future. Some companies pay part of their profit to owners as **[[dividend|dividends]]**.

blocks.tip: The **share price** is just what the last buyer paid. Price × all the shares = the company’s [[market-cap|market value]].

cards.added: Price path between $40 and $50 drawn for the Academy (board shows only the start, end and +25%)
cards.title: Price is not worth
cards.text: Acme’s business didn’t change this month. Same shops, same sales. Its share price still rose 25%.

items.title: Acme share price
items.label: Acme’s share price climbs from $40 to $50 in a month, up 25%

cards.foot: Price moves when buyers are keener than sellers: news, mood, hype. The business can stay exactly the same.

cards.added: Feedback for options the board doesn’t show written for the Academy
cards.title: Which company is bigger?
cards.q: Acme’s shares cost $20. Beta’s shares cost $200. Which company is worth more?

options.feedback: A pricey share doesn’t mean a big company. Market value is price times all the shares.
A cheap share doesn’t make a company big or small. Market value is price times all the shares, and you don’t know the share counts.

options.text: You can’t tell without the share count
options.feedback: Exactly. One share’s price says nothing about size. You need price × all the shares.
Nothing here says they’re equal. Market value is price times all the shares, and the share counts can be very different.

cards.added: Feedback for options the board doesn’t show written for the Academy
cards.title: Up 10%, same business
cards.q: Northwind’s shares rose 10% today. Nothing in the business changed. Why can that happen?

options.feedback: Profit doesn’t change in a day. Price is what buyers pay, and today buyers were keener than sellers.
Price is what buyers pay. Today they were keener than sellers, so the price rose while the business stayed the same.
More shares cut the company into more slices. That tends to push each share’s price down, not up.
That would be a real change in the business. Here nothing changed: buyers were simply keener than sellers.

cards.headline: You know what a share really is.
lines: A share is a slice of ownership.
Price is what buyers pay, not what the business is worth.
Market value = price × all the shares.
